historical_record.description: The south windmill, Murphy's Mill, was built in 1906; the city lists it as a Structure of Merit under Article 10 of the Planning Code.
Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 210, Murphy Windmill and Millwright's Cottage.

Samuel G. Murphy — a North Carolina-born Confederate veteran who had become president of the First National Bank of San Francisco — gave the Park Commission $20,000 for a second windmill to irrigate the park, wishing to see it made "the most beautiful spot in the world".

Designed in 1905 by the consulting mechanical engineer J. C. H. Stutt but delayed by the earthquake, the windmill was built from early 1907: 97 feet tall, a wood-framed octagonal tower of Oregon pine sheathed in slate on a 30-foot concrete base, under a copper dome that turned to the wind, with the longest sails of any windmill built — the stock one 114-foot length of Oregon pine. On completion it was the largest windmill in the world, pumping up to 40,000 gallons an hour to the reservoir on Strawberry Hill.
Electric pumps had replaced the wind-driven ones in both park windmills by this year; the mills were kept as landscape features.

A campaign led since the 1960s by Eleanor Rossi Crabtree, daughter of Mayor Angelo Rossi, had raised $76,000 to save the park's windmills from demolition; it restored the Dutch Windmill, but the Murphy Windmill, stripped of its sails, gallery and fantail, was left unrestored.

unknowns: The Golden Gate Park Master Plan EIR dates Murphy's Mill to 1906; its landmark designation report says it was designed in 1905 and, delayed by the earthquake, built from early 1907.
